name: The Ombu of the Giardino Inglese

location.address: Giardino Inglese, Via della Liberta, Palermo

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), sheet 15/G273/PA/19

verify_notes: MASAF sheet 15/G273/PA/19: Phytolacca dioica ('Fitolacca arborea'), girth 410 cm, height 10 m, criteria age/size, ecological value, rarity; urban context yes. Register is the single official source (also listed in the 2018 first national list per cefalunews). Alive: four Commons photos named Phytolacca dioica Giardino inglese, geotagged 38.133277,13.350979, taken 2026-09-28. Pin confirmed by that geotag (about 17 m from register point 38.13334,13.35109); the pin is the geotagged photo position. Not the same tree as pal_015 (banyan fig, 210 m south-east). Ombu is a South American species; the girth is a swollen, buttressed base. No age source: leave empty. Hours of the park not verified.

photo.note: Looked at the pixels 2026-11-02 (session 9b29504f): the ombu's swollen base and spreading limbs fill the frame; filename names species and garden, geotag 17 m from the register point; daylight, colour (photo_light OK)

story:
Most of the 4.1 metres around this tree is base. The ombu, Phytolacca dioica, comes from South America, and it builds a swollen, buttressed foot that spreads across the ground long before it looks like a trunk. Sicily's register of monumental trees files it as the Fitolacca arborea, gives it that 410-centimetre girth and a height of ten metres, and lists it for its rarity and ecological value as well as its size.

Rarity is the right word in Palermo. The city's big trees are overwhelmingly Moreton Bay figs from Australia, and the Giardino Inglese has its own registered fig about two hundred metres to the south-east. The ombu is the odd one out, a South American tree in a nineteenth-century park on Via della Libertà better known for its figs.

It was photographed in September 2026 for Wiki Loves Monuments, which is how we know it is standing and where. The photographs show the swollen base and limbs spreading low from it, and their position is our pin.

The tree was on Italy's first national list of monumental trees in 2018, which is about all the paper record holds. Nobody has published when it was planted or how old it is. The park is free and on one of the city's main streets. If you know the tree's age, or remember it younger, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the swollen, buttressed base, 4.1 metres round, with low limbs spreading from it, unlike the park's figs; one of them, 8.2 metres round, stands about 200 metres south-east.

story:
Palermo's other registered London plane costs a ticket and stands in a villa garden. This one costs nothing and stands on a pavement beside the wall of the Ucciardone prison, on a busy road north of the port. Sicily's register of monumental trees gives it 28 metres of height and a trunk 4.2 metres round, and lists it for its size and its form.

That is close to the Villa Tasca plane elsewhere on this page, which the register measures at 30 metres and 4.65. The difference is the setting. Villa Tasca's tree has a swan lake and a landscape garden. This one has traffic on one side and the prison wall on the other, and it grew to the same scale anyway.

It was on Italy's first national list of monumental trees in 2018. In September 2026 a photographer for Wiki Loves Monuments stood by it, and the GPS of that photograph falls on the register's own point, so the pin is good. The street is a public road, so there is no gate, no ticket and no closing time. Visitors simply stand on the pavement.

Nobody has published an age or a planting date. A plane this size on a street like this has seen a great deal of the city go by. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, a plane 28 metres tall with a trunk 4.2 metres round, on the pavement of Via Piano dell'Ucciardone beside the prison wall.

name: The Cypress of San Benedetto il Moro

location.address: Convento e Cimitero di Santa Maria di Gesu, Via Santa Maria di Gesu, Monte Grifone, Palermo

location_site.name: Chapel of San Benedetto, Santa Maria di Gesu

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), sheet 04/G273/PA/19

access: In the grounds of the 15th-century convent and monumental cemetery of Santa Maria di Gesù on Monte Grifone; reached from the cemetery by the path up to the chapel of San Benedetto. No ticket mentioned by sources; check opening hours before you go.
transport: Santa Maria di Gesù, south-east Palermo, about 4 km from the centre, above Via Oreto Nuova.
verify_notes: Palermo's tree traditionally called the oldest in the city. MASAF sheet 04/G273/PA/19: girth 350 cm, height 23 m (register point 38.08301,13.37947, same point carried by an OSM node tagged ref:masaf, i.e. a register import, not independent). Other figures: Italian Botanical Heritage (2018 measurement) gives age about 438 years in 2018, height 75.4 ft (23 m), girth 10.3 ft at 6.2 ft above ground (about 314 cm), single trunk leaning against the wall under the chapel, lightning damage, crown 35.4 x 25 ft. Palermo e Palermitani gives 436 years, 23 m, 3.15 m. Balarm (3 March 2021) says an increment core dated it to 444 years and that a broken top is attributed by friars to lightning. Register 350 vs 314-315 cm in other sources: both recorded, the difference is probably the measuring height. Legend: it grew from a stick of Saint Benedict the Moor (1524-1589); a legend, not an age source (it would put the tree at about 440 years, which broadly agrees). Alive: described in 2021 article and measured 2018; no dated photograph or observation found since 2022 (Commons geosearch and iNaturalist returned nothing near the tree; Commons has no matching file found by search), so flagged. Pin approximate: no geotagged photo or GPS found; the small named site is the chapel at the top of the convent park. Olive 047/G273/PA/19 (register 38.08199,13.37980 per brief, OSM import node at 38.08304,13.37846) not verified: no source, no access evidence; see leads. Hours of the cemetery not checked; no ticket mentioned by sources.
story:
Palermo calls this cypress its oldest tree, and in 2021 an increment core put a number on it, 444 years. That is the figure the Palermo news site Balarm reported. The Italian Botanical Heritage guide gave about 438 years when it measured the tree in 2018, and another local site gives 436. Three counts within a decade of each other is as close as old-tree dating gets.

The legend says more. It holds that the cypress grew from a stick planted by Saint Benedict the Moor, who lived from 1524 to 1589, at the convent of Santa Maria di Gesù on Monte Grifone. A legend is not an age, but this one lands in roughly the same place as the core.

The tree has had a hard life. It leans against the wall below the chapel of San Benedetto, and its top is broken, which the friars put down to lightning. It still stands 23 metres tall. Italy's register of monumental trees gives the trunk 3.5 metres round, while the other sources measure about 3.15, probably at a different height.

The route is through the convent's monumental cemetery, up the path to the chapel. The latest account we have of the tree is that 2021 article, and we have not found a dated photograph since. If you have been up recently, tell us how it looks.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the tall cypress with a broken top leaning against the wall below the chapel of San Benedetto, at the top of the Santa Maria di Gesù convent grounds.

name: The Banyan Fig of Villa Niscemi

location.address: Parco di Villa Niscemi, Piazza dei Quartieri 2, Palermo

official_register.name: Elenco degli alberi monumentali d'Italia (MASAF), sheet 30/G273/PA/19

access: Free. Parco di Villa Niscemi is a municipal park, open daily from 9:00 to sunset per the Comune di Palermo tourism portal (other listings give 9:00 to 18:00 or 19:00). The villa is the mayor's representative seat, so access to the building varies.
transport: Piazza dei Quartieri, beside the Favorita park in north-west Palermo.
verify_notes: MASAF sheet 30/G273/PA/19: Ficus macrophylla, girth 3600 cm, height 8 m (a girth of 36 m at 8 m height means a multi-stem, spreading banyan form, not a single trunk; record as a mass of fused trunks and aerial roots). Register only: flagged. No dated sighting since 2022 found (web search, Commons search, iNaturalist near the pin returned nothing); not known dead. Pin approximate: register point 38.16399,13.33353, repeated by an OSM node tagged ref:masaf (a register import, fixme=resurvey). Same park holds 29/G273/PA/19 Ficus microcarpa girth 420 h18 (38.16424,13.33455) and 32/G273/PA/19 Dracaena draco girth 250 h8 (38.16365,13.33341), and 31/G273/PA/19 Ficus microcarpa girth 560 h20 (its OSM node sits at 38.1562,13.3439, 1.3 km off, so the OSM node coordinates are not reliable). Recognise (from the register, not seen): a very wide, low, spreading fig whose width far exceeds its height, with aerial roots; the dragon tree is 30 m south-west of it. No age source.
story:
Italy's register of monumental trees gives this fig a girth of 36 metres and a height of eight. No single trunk is 36 metres round. What the number describes is a Moreton Bay fig that has spread sideways into a mass of fused stems and aerial roots, far wider than it is tall, in the park of Villa Niscemi.

On paper that is a bigger number than the 27 metres the register gives the Villa Tasca fig elsewhere on this page, or any girth given for the Orto Botanico's famous tree. On the ground the comparison does not hold up well, because nobody measures these colonnades the same way twice. Read it as the register's figure for a very wide, very low tree, not as a ranking.

Villa Niscemi sits beside the Favorita park in the north-west of the city and is the mayor's representative seat, but its park is municipal and free, open daily from nine until sunset according to the city's tourism portal. The same park holds a registered dragon tree about thirty metres south-west of the fig and two registered Indian laurel figs.

The record is thin, and we would rather say so. This is register only, our pin is the register's point, and we found no dated photograph or sighting since 2022. Nobody has published an age. If you walk the park, a photograph would settle a lot.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as a very wide, low fig spreading on many fused stems and aerial roots, far wider than its 8 metres of height, with a dragon tree about 30 metres south-west.

verify_notes: MASAF sheet 37/G273/PA/19: Dracaena draco, girth 300 cm, height 8 m, register point 38.11143,13.37320. Owner-managed ground (botanic garden), register is enough. A 2011 garden blog describes a monumental Dracaena draco on a small artificial hill beside a reed hut near the aquarium pond, surrounded by bamboo; the 2023 Commons series is dated and shows a dragon tree in the garden, so one is alive at least as of Feb 2023. Not confirmed these are the same specimen as register 37; the garden may hold several. Different from pal_003, pal_012, pal_017 (other species). Flagged: identity of trunk not settled, pin approximate (garden level). Recognise: stout candelabra crown of stiff blade leaves; look near the aquarium pond area on the hill by the reed hut, per the 2011 blog. No age source: dragon trees have no rings; leave empty.
story:
A dragon tree lays down no growth rings, so nobody can count this one's years. Italy's register of monumental trees gives it a trunk three metres round and a height of eight metres inside Palermo's Orto Botanico, and leaves the age column, like everyone else, empty.

It is the slimmest dragon tree on this page. The ones at Villa Malfitano and the Palazzina Cinese are about six metres round, and the one at the Lo Porto nursery seven. What this one has is company. It grows in the same botanical garden as the 1845 fig that the Piazza Marina tree was grown from, so one ticket covers both.

Finding it takes a little work. A garden blog from 2011 describes a monumental dragon tree on a small artificial hill beside a reed hut near the aquarium pond, ringed with bamboo. Photographs from February 2023 show a dragon tree alive in the garden. Whether these are the register's tree, and not another of its kind, has not been confirmed. The garden may hold more than one, so our pin is the garden rather than the trunk.

If you find it, look for the stout trunk and the candelabra of stiff blade leaves on the hill by the pond, and send us a photograph with your position. That would settle which tree the register meant.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the stout trunk and candelabra crown of stiff blade leaves, on a small hill beside a reed hut near the aquarium pond, ringed with bamboo.
